title: CSS Box Model
subtitle: Understand Space, Size and Structure
description: Build a deep understanding of how CSS elements occupy space. Learn content, padding, border, margin, width, height and box-sizing, then apply them to real dashboard, profile, form and application components.

blocks.text: Welcome to the Box Model
Open your CSS dashboard project.
Before we write new CSS, I want you to look at the interface.
Look at the distance between the text and the edge of each card.
Now look at the distance between one card and the next card.
Those two spaces may look similar, but CSS treats them differently.
Understanding that difference is one of the most important foundations of CSS.
Today you are going to learn how the browser thinks about every element on the page.
The browser essentially treats each element as a box.
That box has content, padding, border and margin.
Once you understand those four layers, many confusing CSS problems become much easier.
1. The Four Parts of Every CSS Box
Imagine that this course card is a physical package.
The information inside the package is the content.
The empty space protecting the information is padding.
The edge surrounding the package is the border.
The space separating the package from another package is the margin.
That mental picture will help you remember the Box Model.

blocks.title: The Four Layers
blocks.output: The content stays inside the card, padding creates internal space, the border creates a boundary, and margin creates external space.

blocks.text: Notice that each property controls a different layer.
Do not memorize the four names without understanding the direction of the space.
Always ask whether the space is inside the element or outside it.
2. Content: The Actual Information
The content area is where the actual information of the element lives.
For a paragraph, the text is content.
For an image element, the image occupies the content area.
For a button, the button label is part of the content.
CSS can control the width and height of that content area.

blocks.title: Controlling a Content Width
blocks.output: The declared content width is 320 pixels under the default content-box model.

blocks.text: The important word here is content.
With the default box-sizing value, width refers to the content area.
Padding and border can then add additional size around that content.
3. Padding: Breathing Room Inside
Now remove the padding from your card.

blocks.title: No Internal Space
blocks.output: The content moves close to the card boundary.

blocks.text: Run the page.
Look at how uncomfortable the card feels.
Now add twenty-four pixels of padding.

blocks.title: Adding Breathing Room
blocks.output: The content moves inward and the card becomes more comfortable to read.

blocks.text: Run it again.
The card did not move away from another card.
Instead, its content moved away from the card's edges.
That is padding.
Padding is internal space.
You will use it constantly in cards, buttons, forms, navigation items and application panels.
4. Padding in Four Directions
Sometimes an interface needs different amounts of space on different sides.

blocks.title: Four Padding Values
blocks.output: The values represent top, right, bottom and left.

blocks.text: The order is top, right, bottom and left.
Think of yourself standing at the top of the element and moving clockwise.
Ten pixels go to the top.
Twenty pixels go to the right.
Thirty pixels go to the bottom.
Forty pixels go to the left.
But you do not always need four values.

blocks.title: Two Padding Values
blocks.output: Twenty pixels are used for top and bottom, while twenty-four pixels are used for left and right.

blocks.text: This shorthand is extremely common in real CSS projects.
5. Margin: Space Outside
Now let's solve a different problem.
Imagine that two course cards are touching each other.

blocks.title: Cards Without Separation
blocks.output: There is no bottom margin separating one card from the next.

blocks.text: Now add twenty pixels.

blocks.title: Separating Cards
blocks.output: A twenty-pixel gap appears outside the bottom of each card.

blocks.text: Run the page.
The content did not move inside the card.
The entire card simply has more space separating it from the next element.
That is margin.
Margin is external space.
6. Padding or Margin?
This is one of the most important decisions you will make while styling interfaces.
Suppose the text inside a card is too close to the edge.
Think padding.
Suppose two cards are too close to each other.
Think margin.
Suppose a button's text is too close to the button's edge.
Think padding.
Suppose two buttons need more separation from each other.
Think margin.
This simple diagnostic habit will make CSS debugging much easier.
7. Border: The Boundary
The border sits between padding and margin.

blocks.title: Creating a Card Boundary
blocks.output: A one-pixel solid border appears around the card.

blocks.text: The first value controls thickness.
The second value controls the border style.
The third value controls the border color.

blocks.title: Changing Border Thickness
blocks.output: The card receives a thicker cyan border.

blocks.text: Run both versions and compare them.
A thicker border becomes more visually dominant.
That is why real interfaces often use subtle borders unless a strong boundary is intentional.
8. Border Radius and Component Shape
Now let's change the shape of the card.

blocks.title: Rounded Card
blocks.output: The card corners become rounded.

blocks.text: Border radius does not create the space between components.
It changes the shape of the element's corners.
That distinction matters.
Padding controls internal space.
Margin controls external space.
Border creates the boundary.
Border radius controls the corner shape.
9. Width, Height and the Real Size of a Box
Now we need to go deeper.
When you write width: 300px, you need to know exactly what that 300 pixels represents.

blocks.title: A Sized Card
blocks.output: Under content-box sizing, the content is 300 pixels wide and padding and borders are added outside that content width.

blocks.text: With the default content-box model, the declared width applies to the content area.
The left and right padding are then added.
The left and right borders are also added.
So the final outer width is larger than the declared content width.
For this example, the horizontal calculation is 300 plus 20 plus 20 plus 2 plus 2.
That gives an outer width of 344 pixels.
This calculation is extremely important when you are trying to understand why elements become wider than expected.
10. box-sizing: border-box
Now we are going to change how the browser calculates the size.

blocks.title: Using Border Box
blocks.output: The complete outer width is 300 pixels, including padding and border.

blocks.text: This is a major difference.
With border-box, the declared width includes the content, padding and border.
The browser has to fit all those layers inside the 300-pixel box.
This makes sizing much easier to predict.
That is one reason border-box is extremely common in modern frontend development.
11. The Global box-sizing Rule
Instead of adding border-box to every component one by one, developers commonly apply it globally.

blocks.title: Predictable Sizing Everywhere
blocks.output: Every element uses border-box sizing.

blocks.text: The star selector targets all elements.
The result is a more predictable sizing system across the page.
You will see this pattern in many real CSS projects.
It becomes especially useful when you start building complex layouts.

Now we are going to build something useful.
Imagine this card belongs to a real learning platform.

blocks.text: Run it.
Look at every space in the card.
The card has space inside.
The card has space outside.
The card has a boundary.
The card has rounded corners.
This is the Box Model being used as part of a real component.
13. Application: Build a Form Field
Now let's use the same knowledge in a form.
Forms appear everywhere in real applications.
Login pages use them.
Registration pages use them.
Shopping platforms use them.
Social applications use them.

blocks.title: Application Form Field
blocks.output: A basic application form field.

blocks.title: Sizing the Input
blocks.output: The input fills the available width and has controlled internal spacing and a visible boundary.

blocks.text: Notice the combination.
The field uses margin to separate itself from the next field.
The input uses padding to create comfortable space around the text.
The border defines the input boundary.
Border-box keeps the width predictable.

blocks.text: The important lesson is not the exact numbers.
The important lesson is knowing why each property exists.
That is how you become capable of building new interfaces without copying someone else's exact design.
15. Application Debugging
Now let's practice thinking like a developer.
Imagine a card looks too crowded.
Do not immediately change random properties.
First identify exactly where the problem is.
If the content is too close to the card edge, check padding.
If two cards are too close together, check margin.
If the boundary is missing, check border.
If the corners are too sharp, check border-radius.
If the element is unexpectedly wide, inspect width, padding, border and box-sizing.
This is how professional debugging begins.

blocks.question: A course card has plenty of space from the next card, but its text is touching the inside edges. Which change directly solves the problem?
options: Increase border width on the card
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The problem is inside the card, so padding is the appropriate solution.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The card already has enough external separation. Focus on the space between its content and its edge.
blocks.reasoning: Padding controls the space between an element's content and its border.
blocks.suggestion: Ask yourself: is the problem inside the card or outside the card?

blocks.question: Two profile cards are touching each other, but their internal content spacing is already comfortable. What should you adjust?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Margin controls external space between components.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The content inside each card is already comfortable. The problem is the distance between separate cards.
blocks.reasoning: Margin creates space outside an element and is commonly used to separate components.
blocks.suggestion: Ignore the content and look only at the gap between the two cards.

blocks.question: A developer writes width: 300px, padding: 20px, and border: 2px solid. With the default content-box model, what is the outer width?
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Remember that content-box adds left and right padding and borders to the declared content width.
blocks.reasoning: Outer width equals content width plus left and right padding plus left and right borders.

blocks.question: A 300px-wide input has 16px horizontal padding and a 1px border on each side. You want the total outer width to remain exactly 300px. Which approach is best?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. border-box includes padding and border inside the declared width.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The goal is to keep the entire outer box at exactly 300px while retaining padding and borders.
blocks.reasoning: border-box makes the declared width include the content, padding and border.
blocks.suggestion: Think about which box-sizing value makes the declared width represent the entire box.

blocks.question: A button label feels cramped against the button edges. Which change is most appropriate?
options: Increase the outside width of the parent
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Padding gives the button's content internal breathing room.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The problem is the distance between the label and the button boundary.
blocks.reasoning: Button padding controls the internal space surrounding its label.
blocks.suggestion: Imagine pushing the label inward while keeping the button in the same general location.

blocks.question: A developer wants a visible line around a card without changing the card's text color. Which property should be used?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Border creates the visible boundary around the card.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The requirement is a boundary around the element, not a change to its text or background.
blocks.reasoning: The border is the Box Model layer that visually surrounds the padding and content.
blocks.suggestion: Think about the line you can see around the outside edge of a card.

blocks.question: A dashboard card is correctly sized, but its corners look too sharp for the application's design. Which property should you change?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. border-radius controls the shape of the corners.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The problem is the shape of the corners, not the amount of internal or external space.
blocks.reasoning: border-radius changes sharp corners into rounded corners.
blocks.suggestion: Look for the CSS property that describes a corner's radius.

blocks.question: You are building a login form. The inputs should fill the available container width, keep their padding inside that width, and remain predictable when borders are added. Which setup is strongest?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. width: 100% fills the container while border-box keeps padding and borders inside that declared width.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The question is specifically about predictable sizing when padding and borders are included.
blocks.reasoning: border-box is useful for full-width form controls because their padding and borders stay inside the declared width.
blocks.suggestion: Focus on the relationship between width, padding and border.

blocks.question: A developer wants every element in the application to use border-box sizing without repeating the rule for every selector. Which rule is most appropriate?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The universal selector targets every element.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about which selector targets all elements on the page.
blocks.reasoning: The universal selector (*) matches all elements.
blocks.suggestion: Which selector have you learned that means 'every element'?

blocks.question: You are debugging a dashboard. The cards look correct individually, but there is not enough space between them. Which sequence is the most logical?
options: Change color, then border-radius, then width
Inspect margin, adjust the external spacing, then run the page again
Increase border thickness until the cards separate
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The problem is external spacing, so inspect and adjust margin.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The cards themselves are fine. Focus on what controls the space between separate elements.
blocks.reasoning: Margin controls external spacing, and testing after the change confirms the result.
blocks.suggestion: Identify the location of the missing space before choosing a property.

blocks.text: 16. Final Challenge: Think Like an Interface Developer
Imagine you are building a complete application.
The application has a navigation bar.
It has course cards.
It has profile cards.
It has forms.
It has buttons.
It may eventually have hundreds of components.
Every one of those components needs predictable spacing and sizing.
That is why the Box Model is not a small CSS topic.
It is one of the foundations of interface construction.
When you understand it deeply, you stop guessing where elements will appear.
You can reason about the space mathematically.
You can identify whether a problem is inside a component or outside it.
You can predict how padding and borders affect dimensions.
You can use border-box to make sizing predictable.
And you can transfer these skills to completely different projects.

blocks.question: You are building a complete dashboard and a card has three problems: its text is too close to its edge, the next card is too close, and the card needs a visible boundary. Which combination directly addresses all three problems?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Padding handles internal space, margin handles external space, and border creates the boundary.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Break the problem into three locations: inside the card, outside the card, and the card's boundary.
blocks.reasoning: Each problem maps directly to a different Box Model layer.
blocks.suggestion: Match each problem to its layer: inside, outside, and boundary.

blocks.text: Lesson Summary
You now understand the four major layers of the CSS Box Model.
Content is the actual information inside an element.
Padding creates space between content and the border.
Border creates the boundary around the element.
Margin creates space outside the element.
Width and height control dimensions.
Box-sizing controls how those dimensions are calculated.
The most important thing is not memorizing isolated properties.
The most important thing is learning how to diagnose a visual problem and choose the correct CSS tool.
That skill will become more valuable as our interfaces become more complex.
HTML gives our application structure.
CSS gives that structure a visual system.
JavaScript will eventually give the interface behavior.
Together, those skills will allow you to build complete websites and applications.
That is the destination we are working toward throughout Code Academy.
Do not just ask whether your code works.
Ask whether you understand why it works.
That is how you move from copying code to becoming someone who can build.
